newsitem.title: UK: Europe takes centre-stage in UK election battle.
newsitem.headline: Europe takes centre-stage in UK election battle.

text.p: Europe returned to centre stage in Britain's election campaign on Friday as Prime Minister John Major attacked the opposition Labour Party's European policies but faced renewed divisions in his own party.

As Labour launched a bid for the votes of British business, Major said opposition leader Tony Blair's pledge to sign up to the European Social Chapter would weaken British companies and threaten thousands of jobs.

But his attempt to seize the initiative on Europe was blunted by reports that a government minister was among dozens of Conservative candidates who had flouted Major's official "wait-and-see" policy on a European single currency and promised voters they would never back monetary union.
The Times said agriculture minister Angela Browning had shown clear opposition to a single currency in a constituency newsletter. But Browning insisted her views were in line with government policy.

"My views are totally compatible with those of this government and the policy in the Conservative Party manifesto," Browing said in a statement. "I have made clear both verbally and in writing that I fully support the prime minister's decision to negotiate and decide."
Labour seized on reports that several Conservative election candidates were defying Major and ruling out joining the single currency in their election addresses to voters.
"The Conservatives are no longer a party, but a rabble," Labour foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook said. "These election addresses are a massive snub to John Major from his colleagues."

Labour was due to launch a special business manifesto in London's financial district on Friday morning as part of its drive to win the votes of Britain's traditionally Conservative business community. The party's national election broadcast on Thursday was also aimed at winning votes from entrepreneurs.
But Major told a rally on Thursday that Blair's policies would damage business and restore the power of Britain's unions.

"If Mr Blair signed the Social Chapter, Britain would be powerless to stop policies that have helped create the worst dole (unemployment) queues in post-war Europe being injected into Britain," Major told supporters in central England.

"The unions have long seen Europe as the back door to power in Britain. While (former premier) Margaret Thatcher and I have been in charge, that back door has stayed firmly bolted. A Labour government would slip that bolt ever so quietly open."

Blair, however, told British radio he would not be bullied by the unions. "Nobody, no interest group, no pressure group, no trade union, no vested interest of any kind is going to stand in the way of me giving the British people the deal I have promised," he said.

The Conservative and Labour parties have a similar stance on many European issues, with both parties declining to commit themselves to joining a single currency in the first wave and choosing instead to "wait and see".
But while the Conservatives have opted out of the Social Chapter, which sets minimum levels of workers' rights across the European Union, Labour says it will sign up if it wins power.
Major urged his supporters to "fight clean, but fight like terriers" and said Labour was in disarray.

"We've seen the Labour Party crumble, crumple and crash to the ground under the first bit of real pressure," he said. "In the next three weeks the Conservative Party will write the biggest news story in modern political history."
But an opinion poll on Friday showed the Conservatives making only a small dent in Labour's commanding lead, in contrast to a survey on Thursday which suggested the gap was narrowing significantly.

The Harris poll in The Independent newspaper showed Labour's lead slipping to 22 points from 24 the previous week. The newspaper said the poll showed that Thursday's signs of a Conservative fightback were "more a statistical wobble than a political earthquake".
